headline: High: Gemini CLI’s filesystem/MCP write access can collide with taipy workflows, creating default-path prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files and use MCP servers, so taipy outputs placed in shared files or a shared workspace could be treated as instructions. Taipy itself has no documented isolation or provenance controls here, so the pair creates a plausible file-mediated injection path, though not a direct one.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or files are exchanged through the filesystem
IF taipy-generated content is later parsed by Gemini CLI as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP servers unless explicitly needed
Require a human review step before Gemini CLI executes file-derived instructions
Prefix taipy outputs as data-only and strip executable-looking directives
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between taipy outputs and Gemini CLI inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment and can egress broadly to Google APIs or user-configured MCP servers. Taipy shows no network egress and no data classes touched, so the main leakage risk is Gemini CLI exporting shared workspace contents; the pair lacks documented isolation to prevent that.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared directory or shell environment
IF Gemini CLI sends those contents to its backend or an MCP server
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared cwd
Run Gemini CLI in a separate user account or container
Disable optional Google account login and unnecessary MCP servers
Rotate any secrets that were already present in the workspace
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI can write the filesystem and modify git state, while taipy is a data-engineering tool with no concurrency or locking details provided. If both touch the same repo or mutable workspace, overlapping writes can conflict; uncertainty about taipy’s write behavior means the safer medium rating is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF taipy performs any concurrent mutation of shared files or state
mitigations: Assign separate branches or directories
Pause one agent before the other mutates git state
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Review and merge changes manually after each run
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can generate code, shell actions, or file edits that taipy may consume in a data-engineering workflow. Taipy has no documented verification gate or critical-evaluation behavior here, so if it treats Gemini output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream work products or automation.
conditions: IF taipy ingests Gemini CLI output as an input artifact or configuration
IF downstream taipy steps execute without independent validation
mitigations: Insert a manual verification step between agents
Require schema validation for any Gemini-produced artifact
Limit Gemini CLI to draft-only outputs
Compare outputs against a known-good baseline before execution
requires-engineering: add automated verification of agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI handles source code, cwd files, and shell environment, while taipy’s profile does not document regulated-data handling or residency constraints. No specific residency or certification mismatch is evidenced, so compliance risk is limited to generic workspace hygiene rather than a documented breach pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF Gemini CLI is used on data subject to stricter residency or retention rules than the surrounding environment
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use separate retention policies for each agent’s outputs
Review vendor/data-processing terms before deployment
Delete transient artifacts after each run
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries
